course.title: Data Literacy
course.description: A practical beginner-to-expert course that teaches every learner to understand, collect, organise, interpret and communicate with data using everyday tools (Excel, Google Sheets, Google Forms). Finish each module check to unlock the next module.

modules.title: Module 1: Understanding data
modules.description: Build a solid foundation: what data is, the main types, and how to judge quality.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: What data is and why it matters
lessons.description: Define data clearly and see why data literacy is a core life and work skill.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain what data is in plain language, give everyday examples, and state why being data-literate matters for your work, business or studies in Uganda.

Why this matters

Every day people make decisions with incomplete or wrong information. A market vendor who does not track which products sell fastest wastes money on stock that sits. A health worker who cannot read a simple table may miss a rising trend. Data literacy is the ability to ask good questions of numbers, words and records so that decisions improve.

What is data?

Data is a record of facts. It can be numbers (sales of 47 units), words (customer names or comments), dates (the day a payment was made), pictures, sound or location. When we organise data and use it to answer a question, it becomes information. When we use that information to decide or act, it becomes knowledge.

Everyday examples in Uganda

  • Mobile-money statements showing inflows and outflows.
  • A school register of attendance.
  • Prices written in a market stall notebook.
  • GPS locations of boda-boda rides.
  • Customer ratings left on a WhatsApp status.

Why data literacy is powerful

It helps you see patterns that are invisible when you rely only on memory or stories. It reduces costly mistakes, supports fair decisions, and makes it easier to explain your work to a boss, a lender or a customer. In a growing digital economy, employers and partners increasingly expect people who can work confidently with data.

Practice

Write down three pieces of data you already collect or could collect this week (for example daily sales, airtime spent, or hours worked). Next to each, write one decision that data could improve.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Types of data
lessons.description: Distinguish quantitative and qualitative data, and discrete versus continuous numbers.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will be able to classify data as quantitative or qualitative, and further as discrete or continuous when it is numerical.

Quantitative data

Quantitative data is numerical. It answers “how many” or “how much”. Examples: number of customers, temperature, revenue in UGX, age, distance in kilometres.

Quantitative data splits into two useful groups:

  • Discrete – countable whole numbers (number of children, number of failed login attempts).
  • Continuous – measured on a scale and can take any value in a range (height, weight, time taken to complete a form).

Qualitative data

Qualitative data describes qualities or categories. It answers “what kind” or “which group”. Examples: gender, district, product colour, customer comment (“the service was slow”), yes/no answers.

Qualitative data is often coded into categories so that it can be counted later (for example “satisfied / neutral / dissatisfied”).

Why the distinction matters

The type of data decides which charts and statistics are valid. You do not calculate an average of colours. You do not usually make a pie chart of continuous height measurements without first grouping them. Knowing the type prevents wrong analysis.

Practice

Classify each of the following: (1) number of boda rides per day, (2) customer satisfaction comment, (3) time in minutes to process a loan, (4) parish name, (5) temperature in degrees Celsius.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3: Data quality and common errors
lessons.description: Recognise incomplete, inaccurate, inconsistent and outdated data and how to reduce these problems.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will be able to name the main dimensions of data quality and spot common errors that make data misleading.

Dimensions of quality

  • Accuracy – the value is correct (the amount recorded matches the real payment).
  • Completeness – required fields are filled; missing values are rare or explained.
  • Consistency – the same thing is recorded the same way every time (dates always as DD/MM/YYYY, names spelled the same).
  • Timeliness – the data is recent enough for the decision you want to make.
  • Uniqueness – no unwanted duplicates.

Common errors in practice

  • Typing 500000 instead of 50 000 (missing or extra zeros).
  • Mixing date formats (05/06/2026 vs 2026-06-05).
  • Recording “Kampala”, “kampala” and “Kla” as three different places.
  • Leaving the gender or age field blank for many respondents.
  • Using an old price list that no longer matches the market.

How to improve quality

Design clear forms, train data collectors, use validation rules in spreadsheets or Google Forms, check a sample of records soon after collection, and keep a short log of any corrections you make.

Practice

Look at any list or register you have (attendance, sales, contacts). Identify two quality problems and write one practical step you can take this week to reduce each problem.

lessons.title: Module 1 review and assessment
lessons.description: Check what you have learned in Module 1. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 1 assessment

You will receive 10 questions drawn from the bank below. Answers are marked immediately with short explanations. The pass mark is 70 %. If you do not pass, review the three lessons and try again.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is data?
*A record of facts such as numbers, words, dates, pictures or sounds
Only numbers typed into a computer
Information that has already been analysed
Opinions written in a report
explain: Data is any recorded fact; analysis turns it into information.
level: 1

Q: Which of the following is qualitative data?
Number of customers served today
*Customer comment “the queue was long”
Total sales in UGX
Average waiting time in minutes
explain: Comments describe quality; the others are numerical.
level: 1

Q: Number of children in a household is an example of:
Continuous quantitative data
*Discrete quantitative data
Qualitative data
A chart type
explain: You count whole children; you cannot have 2.3 children.
level: 2

Q: Which dimension of data quality is harmed when many required fields are left blank?
Accuracy
*Completeness
Timeliness
Uniqueness
explain: Missing values reduce completeness.
level: 1

Q: Recording the same district as “Mukono”, “mukono” and “MUKONO” mainly harms:
Timeliness
*Consistency
Accuracy of the original measurement
Uniqueness of people
explain: Different spellings of the same place make analysis harder.
level: 2

Q: Why does data type matter when choosing a chart?
It does not matter
*Some charts and statistics are only valid for certain types of data
All charts work for every type of data
Only qualitative data can be charted
explain: Averages of categories or pie charts of continuous measures without grouping are usually wrong.
level: 2

Q: Which action improves data quality at the point of collection?
Deleting rows that look strange after analysis
*Using clear form questions and validation rules
Waiting six months before checking any records
Writing everything only on paper with no backup
explain: Prevention at collection is cheaper and more reliable than later cleaning.
level: 2

Q: Height measured in centimetres is best described as:
Discrete data
*Continuous quantitative data
Qualitative data
A database
explain: Height can take many values on a scale.
level: 1

Q: A price list from 2022 used to set 2026 prices mainly fails which quality dimension?
Accuracy of the original 2022 prices
*Timeliness
Completeness
Uniqueness
explain: The data is outdated for current decisions.
level: 2

Q: Turning raw data into a clear answer to a decision question produces:
More raw data
*Information (and with use, knowledge)
Only a chart
A password
explain: Organised, purposeful data becomes information.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 2: Collecting data
modules.description: Plan what to collect, design good questions, and use Google Forms effectively.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Planning what to collect
lessons.description: Start from the decision, not from the form.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will be able to write a clear data-collection plan that starts from the decision you need to make.

Start with the decision

Ask: What decision will this data support? Who will use the results? When do they need them? Only then decide what to measure. Collecting “everything” wastes time and often produces unused, low-quality data.

Key planning questions

  • What is the exact question we need to answer?
  • What population or process are we studying?
  • What is the smallest set of variables that will answer the question?
  • How will we sample or cover the population?
  • Who will collect the data and with what tools?
  • How will privacy and consent be handled?

Practice

Choose a real decision (for example “Should we open the shop one hour earlier?”). Write one clear question the data must answer and list the three most important variables you would collect.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Surveys and questionnaires
lessons.description: Write clear, unbiased questions and choose appropriate response formats.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will write short, clear survey questions that avoid leading the respondent and that produce usable answers.

Good question habits

  • Ask one thing at a time.
  • Use simple language the respondent already knows.
  • Avoid leading or loaded wording (“Don’t you agree that…”).
  • Offer balanced response options.
  • Decide early whether the answer should be open text, single choice, multiple choice, or a number.

Common response formats

  • Yes / No
  • Multiple choice (one answer)
  • Checkboxes (several answers)
  • Rating scale (1–5 or 1–10)
  • Short text or paragraph
  • Number or date

Practice

Rewrite this poor question so it is clear and neutral: “Don’t you think our new packaging is much better and more modern than the old one?”

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Collecting data with Google Forms
lessons.description: Build, share and monitor a simple form that feeds a clean spreadsheet.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will create a Google Form, set useful validation, share it, and view the linked spreadsheet of responses.

Why Google Forms

It is free, works on phones, automatically timestamps responses, and writes every answer into a Google Sheet you can analyse later. Many organisations in Uganda already use Google accounts, so collaboration is easy.

Practical steps

  1. Create a new form and give it a clear title and description.
  2. Add questions of the right type (short answer, multiple choice, etc.).
  3. Turn on “Required” for essential fields.
  4. Use response validation for numbers and email addresses where helpful.
  5. Preview the form on a phone before sharing.
  6. Share the link or embed it; monitor responses in the linked Sheet.

Practice

Build a three-question form (one multiple choice, one number, one short text) about a topic you care about. Submit two test responses and confirm they appear correctly in the spreadsheet.

lessons.title: Module 2 review and assessment
lessons.description: Check Module 2 learning. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 2 assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %. Review the lessons if you need to retake.
lessons.quiz:
Q: The best starting point for a data-collection plan is:
A long list of every possible field
*The decision the data must support
The most advanced tool available
Copying another organisation’s form
explain: Start from the decision; only then choose variables and tools.
level: 1

Q: Which is a characteristic of a good survey question?
It asks two things at once
*It uses simple language and asks one clear thing
It pushes the respondent toward a preferred answer
It is as long as possible
explain: Clarity and neutrality produce better data.
level: 1

Q: A question that begins “Don’t you agree that our prices are fair?” is:
Neutral
*Leading / biased
A good open question
Only suitable for numbers
explain: Leading questions push respondents and distort results.
level: 2

Q: Google Forms is especially useful because:
It requires expensive software
*Responses are written automatically into a spreadsheet
It only works on desktop computers
It cannot set required fields
explain: The linked Sheet makes later analysis straightforward.
level: 1

Q: Which response format is best when a respondent may select several true options?
Single multiple-choice
*Checkboxes
Yes/No only
A single number field
explain: Checkboxes allow more than one selection.
level: 2

Q: Response validation in a form is used to:
Make the form look prettier
*Reduce invalid entries (wrong type or range)
Hide the results from the owner
Force every question to be optional
explain: Validation catches many errors at the point of entry.
level: 2

Q: Collecting far more variables than the decision requires usually:
Improves quality automatically
*Wastes time and often lowers quality
Is required by law
Makes analysis easier
explain: Extra unused fields increase burden and error rates.
level: 2

Q: Before sharing a form widely you should:
Delete the linked spreadsheet
*Preview it on a phone and test submit a few responses
Turn off all required fields
Share only the spreadsheet, not the form
explain: Testing catches problems while they are still easy to fix.
level: 1

Q: Privacy and consent should be considered:
Only after data is published
*During the planning stage
Only for qualitative data
Never for internal forms
explain: Ethical and legal obligations start at design time.
level: 2

Q: A rating scale from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 5 (very satisfied) is mainly:
Qualitative open text
*An ordered categorical / ordinal measure
Continuous height data
A database key
explain: The numbers represent ordered categories of satisfaction.
level: 2

modules.title: Module 3: Organising and managing data
modules.description: Use spreadsheets confidently: structure, clean, sort, filter and protect data.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.1: Spreadsheet basics in Microsoft Excel
lessons.description: Rows, columns, cells, basic formulas and good layout habits.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will navigate an Excel worksheet, enter data cleanly, and use simple formulas (SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT).

Core ideas

  • Each column should hold one variable (Date, Amount, Product).
  • Each row should hold one observation (one sale, one student, one day).
  • Keep a header row and freeze it so labels stay visible.
  • Avoid merged cells in the data block; they break sorting and filtering.

Essential formulas

=SUM(B2:B100), =AVERAGE(C2:C50), =COUNT(A2:A100), =COUNTA(A2:A100) for non-empty cells. Always check that the range is correct.

Practice

Create a small sheet with Date, Item, Quantity, Unit Price and a Total column that multiplies Quantity × Unit Price. Add a SUM at the bottom for total value.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.2: Working with Google Sheets
lessons.description: Collaborate, share safely, and use the same core skills in the browser.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will perform the same core spreadsheet tasks in Google Sheets and share a sheet with appropriate permissions.

Why Google Sheets matters

It is free, works offline on phones after setup, and makes real-time collaboration easy. Many teams in Uganda already live inside Google Workspace.

Sharing wisely

Give “Viewer” rights when people only need to read; give “Editor” only to those who must change data. Avoid “Anyone with the link can edit” for sensitive information.

Practice

Upload or recreate the small sales sheet from the previous lesson in Google Sheets. Share it with a colleague as Viewer and confirm they cannot edit.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.3: Cleaning, sorting and filtering data
lessons.description: Turn messy tables into reliable analysis-ready data.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will remove duplicates, fix inconsistent spellings, handle blanks, and use Sort and Filter to explore a table.

Typical cleaning steps

  1. Make a working copy; never overwrite the only original.
  2. Standardise text (trim spaces, consistent capitalisation, agreed spellings of places and products).
  3. Convert numbers stored as text into real numbers.
  4. Decide how to treat blanks (leave, fill with a code, or exclude).
  5. Remove or flag exact duplicate rows.

Sort and Filter

Sort helps you see extremes and groups. Filter lets you focus on one product, one district or one date range without deleting rows.

Practice

Take any messy list you have. Clean three problems (extra spaces, mixed spellings, blanks) and then filter to one category of interest.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.4: Keeping data safe and well organised
lessons.description: Backups, access control, file naming and simple version discipline.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will apply basic practices that protect data from loss, unauthorised access and confusion.

Practical rules

  • Keep at least one backup in a different place (cloud + local, or two different cloud accounts).
  • Use clear file names that include the topic and date (Sales_Kampala_2026-06.xlsx).
  • Limit edit rights; prefer view-only links when possible.
  • Do not put passwords or national ID numbers in ordinary shared sheets.
  • When you make major changes, save a dated version so you can go back.

Practice

Review the files on your phone or computer. Rename two important data files so the name shows content and date, and confirm you have a backup of each.

lessons.title: Module 3 review and assessment
lessons.description: Check Module 3 learning. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 3 assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: In a well-structured data table each column should contain:
Several different variables mixed together
*One variable only
Only charts
Only formulas
explain: One variable per column keeps analysis reliable.
level: 1

Q: Which formula adds the numbers in cells B2 to B20?
=ADD(B2:B20)
*=SUM(B2:B20)
=TOTAL(B2:B20)
=B2+B20 only
explain: SUM is the standard aggregation function.
level: 1

Q: Before cleaning a dataset you should:
Overwrite the only original file
*Make a working copy and keep the original safe
Delete all blank rows immediately
Share the file with “anyone can edit”
explain: Always preserve an untouched original.
level: 1

Q: Freezing the header row is useful because:
It deletes duplicate rows
*Labels stay visible while you scroll
It converts text to numbers
It creates a chart automatically
explain: Frozen headers keep context on screen.
level: 2

Q: Giving a colleague “Viewer” permission means they can:
Change any cell
*See the data but not change it
Delete the whole file
Change sharing settings
explain: Viewer is read-only.
level: 1

Q: Inconsistent spellings of the same place name mainly harm:
File size
*The ability to group and summarise correctly
The colour of charts
Internet speed
explain: Analysis tools treat different spellings as different places.
level: 2

Q: A clear file name should ideally include:
Only the word “final”
*Topic and date (and sometimes version)
The password
Only the author’s first name
explain: Topic + date makes later retrieval reliable.
level: 2

Q: Filter in a spreadsheet is used to:
Permanently delete rows you do not like
*Temporarily show only rows that match chosen criteria
Convert numbers to text
Create a backup
explain: Filtering hides rows without deleting them.
level: 1

Q: Putting national ID numbers in a widely shared “anyone with the link can edit” sheet is:
Best practice
*A serious privacy and security risk
Required by Google
Only a problem for qualitative data
explain: Sensitive personal data needs strict access control.
level: 2

Q: The main reason to avoid merged cells inside a data block is:
They look colourful
*They break sorting, filtering and many formulas
They increase file size dramatically
They are required for charts
explain: Merged cells interfere with normal table operations.
level: 2

modules.title: Module 4: Interpreting data
modules.description: Read tables and charts carefully and turn findings into decisions.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.1: Reading tables and summaries
lessons.description: Extract the right numbers and notice what is missing.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will read a simple table, identify totals, averages and extremes, and notice gaps or odd values.

How to read a table systematically

  1. Read the title and the period it covers.
  2. Identify the units (UGX, percentages, counts).
  3. Look at column and row headers.
  4. Find the totals or key summary rows.
  5. Scan for the largest and smallest values.
  6. Ask what is missing or unclear.

Practice

Open any table of numbers you have (sales by day, attendance by class). Write three factual statements that are directly supported by the table and one question the table does not answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.2: Basic charts and what they show
lessons.description: Choose and interpret bar, line and pie charts correctly.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will select an appropriate chart type and correctly describe what a chart does and does not show.

Common chart types

  • Bar chart – compare quantities across categories.
  • Line chart – show change over time.
  • Pie chart – show parts of a whole (use sparingly; many categories become hard to read).

Reading rules

Always check the scale, the units, the time period and the source. A chart can be accurate yet still misleading if the scale is truncated or categories are ordered oddly.

Practice

Find one chart online or in a report. Write one sentence describing the main message and one possible way the chart could mislead a casual reader.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.3: From data to a simple decision
lessons.description: Turn a clear finding into a practical recommendation.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will move from “what the numbers show” to “what we should do next”, while staying honest about uncertainty.

A simple decision frame

  1. State the original question.
  2. State the key finding in one sentence.
  3. Note any important limitations (small sample, missing days, old data).
  4. Recommend one concrete next action.
  5. Say how you will check whether the action worked.

Practice

Using a finding from your own data or a public table, write a five-line decision note that follows the frame above.

lessons.title: Module 4 review and assessment
lessons.description: Check Module 4 learning. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 4 assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: When reading a table, the first things to check are:
Only the biggest number
*Title, period, units and headers
The font colour
Whether it is printed or digital
explain: Context comes before the numbers.
level: 1

Q: A line chart is usually best for:
Comparing five unrelated categories
*Showing change over time
Displaying parts of a single whole
Listing names alphabetically
explain: Lines emphasise trends across time.
level: 1

Q: A pie chart becomes hard to read when:
There are only two slices
*There are many small categories
The data are continuous measurements without grouping
Both of the above can be true
explain: Too many slices or inappropriate data type both cause problems.
level: 2

Q: Truncating the vertical axis of a bar chart can:
Never change the message
*Make small differences look dramatic
Improve accuracy of the underlying data
Remove the need for a title
explain: Scale choices can exaggerate or hide differences.
level: 2

Q: A good decision note should include:
Only the recommendation
*The question, the finding, limitations, recommendation and a check
Personal opinions only
Every raw data row
explain: Transparent reasoning builds trust and better decisions.
level: 1

Q: Noticing what a table does not show is:
A waste of time
*An important part of careful reading
Only for statisticians
Impossible with digital tables
explain: Gaps and missing variables often matter as much as the numbers present.
level: 2

Q: Bar charts are especially useful for:
*Comparing quantities across categories
Showing exact continuous distributions without grouping
Replacing all tables forever
Hiding the units
explain: Categories map naturally to bars.
level: 1

Q: If a chart has no source or date, you should:
Trust it completely
*Treat it with extra caution
Assume it is from this year
Use it only for pie charts
explain: Provenance is part of credibility.
level: 2

Q: Turning a finding into a decision always requires:
Ignoring uncertainty
*Acknowledging limitations and proposing a way to check the result
Waiting for perfect data
Using only pie charts
explain: Honest uncertainty and follow-up improve outcomes.
level: 2

Q: The main message of a chart should be:
Hidden in the colours
*Stated clearly so a busy reader can grasp it quickly
Left for the reader to invent
Written only in a separate password-protected file
explain: Clarity is the purpose of visualisation.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 5: Describing and visualising data
modules.description: Use averages, spread, percentages and charts to tell a clear story.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.1: Averages – mean, median and mode
lessons.description: Choose and interpret the right average for the situation.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will calculate and interpret mean, median and mode, and know when each is most appropriate.

Definitions

  • Mean – sum of values divided by how many there are. Sensitive to extreme values.
  • Median – the middle value when data are ordered. Robust to outliers.
  • Mode – the most frequent value. Useful for categories or for spotting the most common number.

When to prefer which

Use the median for income or prices when a few very large values would pull the mean up. Use the mean when values are reasonably symmetric and every observation should influence the result equally. Use the mode for the most common category or size.

Practice

For the set 10, 12, 12, 15, 100 calculate mean, median and mode. Which best describes a “typical” value and why?

lessons.title: Lesson 5.2: Spread, ranges and outliers
lessons.description: Describe how spread out the data are and spot unusual values.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will calculate a simple range, recognise outliers, and explain why spread matters as much as the average.

Why spread matters

Two shops can have the same average daily sales, yet one is stable and the other swings wildly. Decisions about stock, staffing and risk depend on spread, not only on the average.

Simple measures

  • Range = maximum − minimum.
  • Outliers are values that sit unusually far from the rest; always investigate before deleting them.

Practice

Find the range of a small set of numbers you care about. Identify any value that looks unusual and write one possible real-world reason for it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.3: Percentages, ratios and fair comparisons
lessons.description: Compare groups of different sizes fairly.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will use percentages and simple ratios so that comparisons between groups of different sizes are fair.

Key idea

Raw counts can mislead when group sizes differ. “20 complaints from Branch A and 5 from Branch B” looks worse for A until you learn A served 2 000 customers and B served 100. Percentages or rates put the numbers on a common scale.

Practice

Invent or use real numbers for two groups of different sizes. Compute a percentage or rate for each and state which group performs better on that measure.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.4: Telling the story with charts and dashboards
lessons.description: Combine a few clear visuals and short text into a useful summary.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will design a simple one-page summary that a busy colleague can understand in under a minute.

Good dashboard habits

  • One main question per view.
  • Most important number or chart at the top left.
  • Consistent colours and units.
  • Short plain-language titles and annotations.
  • Source and date visible.

Practice

Using any small dataset, sketch (on paper or screen) a one-page summary with a title, one key number, one chart and two bullet findings.

lessons.title: Module 5 review and assessment
lessons.description: Check Module 5 learning. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 5 assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: The mean is calculated by:
Taking the middle value
*Adding the values and dividing by how many there are
Finding the most common value
Subtracting the minimum from the maximum
explain: Mean is the arithmetic average.
level: 1

Q: When a few very large values would pull the average up, it is often better to report the:
Mode only
*Median
Range only
Colour of the chart
explain: The median is resistant to extreme values.
level: 2

Q: The mode is:
Always the same as the mean
*The most frequent value
The difference between max and min
Only used for continuous data
explain: Mode = most common observation.
level: 1

Q: Range is defined as:
Mean minus median
*Maximum minus minimum
The number of observations
The most common category
explain: Range is a simple measure of spread.
level: 1

Q: Comparing raw complaint counts between a large and a small branch without rates or percentages is:
Always fair
*Often misleading
Required by law
Only a problem for pie charts
explain: Different group sizes require rates or percentages for fair comparison.
level: 2

Q: An outlier should be:
Always deleted immediately
*Investigated before any decision to keep, correct or exclude it
Ignored in every analysis
Used as the only average
explain: Outliers can be errors or important real events.
level: 2

Q: A good one-page data summary should:
Contain every raw row
*Highlight the main question, key number, one clear chart and short findings
Use as many colours as possible
Hide the source and date
explain: Clarity and focus serve the busy reader.
level: 1

Q: Spread matters because:
Only the average ever affects decisions
*Two groups with the same average can have very different risk or stability
It is the same as the mode
Charts cannot show spread
explain: Variation drives risk and operational decisions.
level: 2

Q: Percentages are especially useful when:
All groups are exactly the same size
*You need to compare groups of different sizes fairly
You want to hide the original counts forever
Data are only qualitative
explain: Percentages put different-sized groups on a common scale.
level: 1

Q: The most important number or chart on a dashboard should usually appear:
In the smallest font at the bottom
*Near the top / in a prominent position
Only in a password-protected second sheet
In a different file
explain: Visual hierarchy guides the reader’s attention.
level: 2

modules.title: Module 6: Introduction to data analytics
modules.description: Move from literacy to the first steps of analysis, ethics and a small capstone project.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.1: What is data analytics?
lessons.description: See the bigger picture of turning data into decisions at scale.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will explain what data analytics is and how it builds on the literacy skills already learned.

Definition

Data analytics is the systematic process of inspecting, cleaning, transforming and modelling data in order to discover useful information, support conclusions and drive decision-making. Literacy is the foundation; analytics adds more powerful tools and a repeatable process.

Practice

In one sentence, explain to a non-technical friend the difference between “looking at a spreadsheet” and “doing data analytics”.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.2: The four types of analytics
lessons.description: Descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive – what each answers.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will name the four common types of analytics and match each to the kind of question it answers.

The four types

  • Descriptive – What happened? (summaries, dashboards)
  • Diagnostic – Why did it happen? (drill-down, comparisons)
  • Predictive – What is likely to happen next? (forecasts, models)
  • Prescriptive – What should we do about it? (recommendations, optimisation)

Practice

Write one example question for each of the four types, related to a shop, school or clinic you know.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.3: The data analytics process
lessons.description: A practical sequence from question to communication.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will list the main stages of a simple analytics process and know what belongs in each stage.

A practical sequence

  1. Clarify the question and success criteria.
  2. Obtain and explore the data.
  3. Clean and prepare the data.
  4. Analyse (summarise, visualise, model if needed).
  5. Interpret results in context.
  6. Communicate findings and recommended actions.
  7. Review what worked and what to improve next time.

Practice

Take a small real question and write one concrete action you would take at each of the first four stages.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.4: Tools and career paths in analytics
lessons.description: See common tools and realistic next steps after this course.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will recognise widely used tools and outline one realistic learning or career step that builds on data literacy.

Common tools

  • Spreadsheets (Excel, Google Sheets) – still the everyday workhorse.
  • SQL – for querying databases.
  • Python or R – for more flexible analysis and automation.
  • Power BI, Looker Studio, Tableau – for interactive dashboards.

Possible next steps

Deepen spreadsheet skills, learn basic SQL, take an introductory Python for data course, or apply data literacy inside your current job to improve a real process.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.5: Data ethics, privacy and responsible use
lessons.description: Protect people while still learning from data.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will apply basic ethical principles when collecting, analysing and sharing data about people.

Core principles

  • Collect only what you need.
  • Be transparent about purpose where possible.
  • Protect personal data (access control, aggregation, anonymisation).
  • Do not use data to harm or unfairly discriminate.
  • Correct errors when you find them.
  • Keep data only as long as necessary.

Practice

Review one data activity you do (or plan to do). Identify one privacy risk and one concrete step to reduce it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.6: Capstone – your first data analysis project
lessons.description: Apply the whole course to a small real project.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will complete a short end-to-end project that demonstrates data literacy from question to recommendation.

Suggested structure

  1. Choose a clear question that matters to you.
  2. Collect or assemble a small dataset (even 20–50 rows is enough).
  3. Clean and organise it in a spreadsheet.
  4. Produce at least one summary table and one chart.
  5. Write a one-page note: question, key finding, limitation, recommendation, how you will check the result.

Success looks like

A colleague who was not involved can understand your question, your main finding and your recommended next step in under two minutes.

lessons.title: Module 6 review and assessment
lessons.description: Final module check for Data Literacy. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 6 assessment

10 questions covering the whole module. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Data analytics primarily aims to:
Store as much data as possible forever
*Turn data into useful information and support better decisions
Replace all human judgement
Only create colourful charts
explain: The purpose is insight and better decisions.
level: 1

Q: “What happened last month?” is mainly a:
*Descriptive question
Predictive question
Prescriptive question
Database question
explain: Descriptive analytics summarises the past.
level: 1

Q: “What is likely to happen to sales next month?” is mainly:
Descriptive
Diagnostic
*Predictive
A chart type
explain: Predictive analytics forecasts future outcomes.
level: 2

Q: The first stage of a practical analytics process should be:
Building the most advanced model
*Clarifying the question and success criteria
Publishing the dashboard
Deleting outliers
explain: Clear questions prevent wasted effort.
level: 1

Q: Which tool is still the everyday workhorse for many analysts?
Only supercomputers
*Spreadsheets such as Excel or Google Sheets
Paper only
Social media apps
explain: Spreadsheets remain central for many tasks.
level: 1

Q: Collecting far more personal data than needed mainly violates:
Chart colour rules
*The principle of data minimisation / need-to-know
The need for backups
File-naming conventions
explain: Ethical practice collects only what is required.
level: 2

Q: Aggregating results and hiding very small groups helps to:
Make charts prettier
*Protect individual privacy
Increase the mean
Remove the need for titles
explain: Small counts can re-identify people.
level: 2

Q: A good capstone project for this course should include:
Only raw data rows
*A clear question, cleaned data, at least one summary and chart, and a short recommendation note
A full machine-learning pipeline
A password-protected video
explain: End-to-end thinking from question to action is the goal.
level: 1

Q: Prescriptive analytics focuses on:
Only describing the past
*Recommending actions
Deleting all data after one use
Choosing chart colours
explain: Prescriptive work answers “what should we do?”.
level: 2

Q: Keeping personal data longer than necessary:
Is always required
*Increases privacy and security risk
Improves the median automatically
Is the same as making a backup
explain: Retention should match purpose and legal needs.
level: 2
